name: Intel TBB
workload: Sum of a 1 GB array (268435456 floats) with std::reduce(std::execution::par) running on the oneTBB backend versus a hand-written reduction that spawns and joins std::thread workers on each call, each worker using a SIMD kernel.
claimed_speedup: AWS Graviton4 c8g.metal-24xl: std::reduce<par>/f32 1950894 ns (550.384 GB/s) versus neon/f32/std::threads 3321599 ns (323.261 GB/s), about 1.7x (derived from page data). AWS Zen4 m7a.metal-48xl: std::reduce<par, f32> 2913596 ns versus avx2<f32aligned>@threads 9612120 ns, about 3.3x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12 (stated in README for the AWS runs); CMake Release build, CMakeLists.txt appends -O2 to the Release flags; the -march=native -fopenmp line is stored in CMAKE_GCC_FLAGS, a variable CMake does not use, so it probably does not apply; oneTBB is fetched from uxlfoundation/oneTBB branch master (unpinned) and USE_INTEL_TBB defaults ON on Linux without CUDA
hardware: AWS Graviton4 c8g.metal-24xl (96 cores at 2000 MHz) for the headline row; AWS Zen4 m7a.metal-48xl (192 threads at 3701.95 MHz, exact CPU SKU not stated) for the second row
tradeoffs: Runtime library dependency (libtbb) and its own task and arena API; work-stealing scheduler tuned for throughput, with per-call scheduling overhead on tiny inputs (not measured here).
caveats: Weak and indirect: the benchmark never calls the TBB API. TBB only runs underneath libstdc++'s std::reduce(std::execution::par), and the README presents the rows as a general comparison, not as a TBB claim. The std::thread baseline spawns and joins cores-1 threads inside every call (threads_gt::operator() in reduce_cpu.hpp), so it pays thread creation each time; pool-based rows on the same machine, fork_union at 1889686 ns and OpenMP at 1901684 ns on Graviton4, match or beat std::reduce<par>. The std::thread rows also use float partial sums (error 1.04 percent on Graviton4, 0.52 percent on Zen4) while std::reduce<par> shows 0. Single README pastes with no repetitions reported, oneTBB master not pinned, Zen4 CPU SKU not stated, README labels the thread rows '@threads' while the source labels them std::threads. No direct tbb::parallel_for or tbb::parallel_reduce comparison and no oneTBB-vs-std::thread number from the oneTBB repository, which has no benchmark directory and no performance figures in its README.

name: Intel Parallel STL
workload: Sum of a 1 GB array (268435456 floats or doubles) with std::reduce(std::execution::par) versus serial std::accumulate, Google Benchmark, TBB-backed parallel algorithms in GCC.
claimed_speedup: AWS Graviton4 c8g.metal-24xl: std::reduce<par>/f32 1950894 ns (550.384 GB/s) versus std::accumulate/f32 192162701 ns (5.58767 GB/s), about 98x (derived from page data); f64 1959062 ns versus 192266754 ns, about 98x (derived from page data). AWS Zen4 m7a.metal-48xl: std::reduce<par, f32> 2913596 ns versus std::accumulate<f32> 219734340 ns, about 75x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12 (stated in README for the AWS runs); CMake Release build, CMakeLists.txt appends -O2 to the Release flags; the -march=native -fopenmp line is stored in CMAKE_GCC_FLAGS, a variable CMake does not use, so it probably does not apply; oneTBB is fetched from uxlfoundation/oneTBB branch master (unpinned) and USE_INTEL_TBB defaults ON on Linux without CUDA
hardware: AWS Graviton4 c8g.metal-24xl (96 cores at 2000 MHz) for the headline row; AWS Zen4 m7a.metal-48xl (192 threads at 3701.95 MHz, exact CPU SKU not stated) for the second row
stars_or_usage: 777 stars on uxlfoundation/oneDPL, which github.com/intel/parallelstl now serves; Parallel STL is the basis of the C++17 parallel algorithms in GCC libstdc++ (background knowledge, not verified on a page opened this session)
tradeoffs: Parallel backend needs oneTBB at link time. The standalone intel/parallelstl repository now serves the oneDPL repository (oneAPI DPC++ Library, Apache-2.0 with LLVM exceptions), which targets SYCL devices and needs the oneAPI toolchain for the device parts.
caveats: Indirect evidence: the benchmark runs libstdc++'s bundled <execution> implementation (a vendored copy of Parallel STL, backed by oneTBB), not a build of intel/parallelstl or oneDPL, so the link to this repository rests on lineage. Serial baseline versus a 96 to 192 thread run on a memory-bandwidth-bound sum, so the order of magnitude says little about library quality. std::accumulate<f32> shows 93.75 percent error because it sums floats serially; the f64 row is accurate. On Graviton4 the hand-written OpenMP (neon/f32/openmp 1901684 ns) and fork_union (neon/f32/av::fork_union 1890173 ns) rows match or beat std::reduce<par>/f32 at 1950894 ns. Single README pastes (no repetitions or variance reported), oneTBB master not pinned, and the benchmark repository has no LICENSE file. DGX-H100 rows in the same README (std::reduce<par, f32> 3749938 ns versus std::accumulate<f32> 194089563 ns) were not used because CUDA machines default USE_INTEL_TBB to OFF, so the backend there is unclear. No comparison against GNU parallel mode, MSVC STL or libc++ parallel algorithms. The README tables were hand-pasted and use older row labels than reduce_bench.cpp.
